artifact.title: Next.js Ping Pong Game — Implementation Plan

nodes.title: Product goal
nodes.text: Build a fast, responsive browser Ping Pong game using Next.js, TypeScript, and Canvas 2D. The first release supports one player versus CPU and local two-player mode, works with keyboard and touch controls, and requires no account or backend.

nodes.title: MVP scope
nodes.text: Keep the first release small enough to validate game feel before adding network complexity.

rows: Responsive court, HUD, pause, sound toggle

nodes.title: Application architecture
nodes.text: Keep the deterministic game engine independent from React so physics can be tested without rendering.

data.summary: A small client-side game shell coordinates input, a pure simulation engine, Canvas rendering, and an accessible DOM HUD.

flow.label: Dual output
flow.detail: Canvas court plus semantic DOM HUD

items: game/input.ts — keyboard, pointer, and touch normalization
components/GameHud.tsx — score, pause, status, and controls
game/audio.ts — optional effects respecting mute preferences

nodes.title: Technical contracts
nodes.text: Define boundaries before visual polish so gameplay remains predictable and testable.

rows: Advance state from elapsed time and input
Fixed simulation step; clamp long frames
Normalize keyboard and touch into actions
No game rules inside event handlers
Draw the latest state onto Canvas
Mount, pause, restart, resize, announce scores
Never set React state every animation frame

nodes.title: Phased implementation
nodes.text: Complete each phase only when its exit checks pass.

items.label: Phase 1 · Project foundation
items.detail: Create the Next.js App Router project, TypeScript configuration, test setup, responsive page shell, and core design tokens.

items.label: Phase 2 · Deterministic engine
items.detail: Define serializable game state and implement the fixed-step loop, paddle movement, serves, scoring, match completion, and deterministic fixtures.

items.label: Phase 3 · Collision system
items.detail: Implement wall and paddle collision response, penetration correction, bounded rebound angles, velocity caps, and edge-case unit tests.

items.label: Phase 4 · Playable responsive interface
items.detail: Add Canvas rendering, coordinate scaling, resize handling, semantic score HUD, keyboard/touch controls, pause/restart, and both local game modes.

items.label: Phase 5 · CPU, game feel, and accessibility
items.detail: Add CPU profiles, speed and rebound tuning, sound controls, reduced motion, high-contrast cues, focus management, status announcements, and mobile resilience.

items.label: Phase 6 · Verification and release candidate
items.detail: Pass engine, component, browser, performance, responsive, accessibility, and real-device gates, then produce the static export candidate.

nodes.title: Delivery dependencies
nodes.text: The order protects the core loop from UI-driven rewrites.

nodes.title: Definition of done
nodes.text: The MVP is complete only when gameplay and product-quality gates pass together.

items: Steady 60 FPS target on supported desktop and mobile browsers
No ball tunnelling through a paddle under maximum configured speed
Keyboard and touch can start, play, pause, resume, and restart
Canvas resizes without distorting gameplay coordinates
Score and game state are available outside Canvas to assistive technology
The game pauses when the document becomes hidden
Reduced-motion mode removes nonessential flashes and camera effects
Unit tests cover serves, collisions, scoring, and match completion
Playwright covers both modes, pause/restart, viewport changes, and touch input
Production build and static export complete without runtime server dependencies

nodes.title: Physics instability
nodes.text: Variable frame times can cause missed collisions, impossible rebound angles, or different outcomes across devices.

data.mitigation: Use a fixed simulation timestep with an accumulator, clamp large elapsed intervals, resolve overlap after collision, cap velocity, and unit-test boundary cases.

nodes.title: Rendering and input performance
nodes.text: Updating React state on every animation frame or mixing layout reads with drawing can create jank and delayed controls.

data.mitigation: Keep frame state in the engine and refs, render through requestAnimationFrame, batch resize measurements, update the DOM HUD only when semantic values change, and profile long tasks.

nodes.title: Mobile usability
nodes.text: Small touch targets, browser gestures, changing viewport height, and fingers covering the court can make a technically working game frustrating.

data.mitigation: Use large separated control regions, pointer events with touch-action rules, dynamic viewport units, safe-area padding, landscape and portrait layouts, and real-device testing.

nodes.title: Delivery risk map
nodes.text: Prioritize technical risk reduction before presentation polish.

data.summary: Physics instability and rendering performance are the highest-priority engineering risks; mobile usability requires early device validation.

nodes.title: Testing strategy
nodes.text: Use Vitest for pure engine and physics tests, React component tests for controls and HUD behavior, and Playwright for complete browser flows. Test deterministic engine fixtures at multiple frame cadences, validate responsive layouts at 375, 768, 1024, and 1440 pixels, and include keyboard-only and touch-emulated runs.

nodes.title: Explicit non-goals
nodes.text: Do not add authentication, databases, real-time networking, matchmaking, chat, payments, analytics tracking, or a complex state-management library in the MVP. Online multiplayer should begin as a separate architecture decision after local gameplay is proven.

nodes.title: Recommended delivery approach
nodes.text: Build the local deterministic MVP first and make game feel measurable before introducing online state. Use the Next.js App Router for the page shell, a narrow client component for browser interactivity, a pure TypeScript engine, Canvas 2D for the court, and semantic DOM controls for accessibility.

nodes.title: Implementation scope decision
nodes.text: Approve the plan before any game code is created.

value.label: Phase 1 · Project foundation
value.detail: Create the Next.js App Router project, TypeScript configuration, test setup, responsive page shell, and core design tokens.

value.label: Phase 2 · Game-state model
value.detail: Define serializable ball, paddle, score, match, difficulty, and input state with explicit defaults and reset rules.

value.label: Phase 3 · Deterministic simulation
value.detail: Build the fixed-step loop, paddle movement, serves, scoring, match completion, and deterministic engine fixtures.

value.label: Phase 4 · Collision system
value.detail: Implement wall and paddle collision response, penetration correction, bounded rebound angles, velocity caps, and edge-case unit tests.

value.label: Phase 5 · Responsive court
value.detail: Add the Canvas renderer, coordinate scaling, resize handling, semantic DOM score HUD, and stable animation lifecycle.

value.label: Phase 6 · Controls and local modes
value.detail: Normalize keyboard, pointer, and touch input; add pause, resume, restart, player-versus-CPU, and local two-player flows.

value.label: Phase 7 · CPU and game feel
value.detail: Add three CPU profiles, progressive speed tuning, sound controls, readable feedback, and measurable gameplay tuning tools.

value.label: Phase 8 · Accessibility and resilience
value.detail: Add reduced motion, high-contrast cues, focus management, status announcements, visibility pause, safe-area support, and real-device checks.

value.label: Phase 9 · Verification and release candidate
value.detail: Pass engine, component, browser, performance, responsive, and accessibility gates, then produce the static export candidate.
